newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: LG-Caltex raises stakes in South Korea petrol war.
newsitem.headline: LG-Caltex raises stakes in South Korea petrol war.

text.p: Conservative LG-Caltex Oil Corp surprised South Korea's refineries on Friday, slashing petrol pump prices to the lowest in the land and raising the stakes in a price war.
Petrol prices have been falling at South Korean pumps since March in what industry analysts have called a price war after the government freed price controls on January 1.
Since deregulation, LG Caltex has offered the highest pump prices in the country.
But it suddenly cut them on Friday and signalled to rivals that it intends to keep them the lowest available to motorists.
"Our ultimate goal is to win additional market share," said a spokesman.

"We also want to remove a set image as a company that sells the most expensive petrol...We intend to keep our petrol prices at the lowest level. If others try to undercut our prices, we could go even lower," he said.
LG-Caltex lowered retail petrol prices to 825 won (93 cents) per litre from 833 won -- which had been the highest previously offered.
The 600,000 barrels-per-day refiner holds the second largest share of the domestic petrol market at 31.7 percent. Yukong Ltd's has the biggest market share at 37.5 percent, analysts said.
The two companies had previously sold petrol at the highest forecourt prices in the land.
Ssangyong Oil Refining Co and Hyundai Oil Refinery Co currently sell petrol for 828 won per litre, while Hanwha Energy Co Ltd sells at 827 won.
Now, the refiners, startled by LG-Caltex's move, are deciding whether they should follow suit.

"We are holding an emergency meeting to examine the situation," said an official at Yukong, the country's largest refiner with production capacity of 810,000 bpd. "We'll decide soon what measure to take."
Analysts said an economic downturn in South Korea has made car drivers more sensitive to petrol prices.
But analysts said they doubted a price war could be sustained.
"It is expected to clear up in the third quarter," said Kim. "The price war will impose a huge cut in profits of oil companies already in a weak financial status. They can't prolong this very long."
Profits of South Korean refiners were savaged last year, largely as a result of foreign exchange losses.
And expansion work has resulted in a larger supply of petrol at a time of falling domestic demand, while at the same time creating debts for the companies.
Analysts said it was difficult to see what refiners would gain from a price war.
"Everyone could end up losers," said Kim Sang-bae, an energy analyst at Ssangyong Investment Securities.
But at the same time, "Local demand hasn't been able to keep up with the capacity expansion," Kim said, "so it's crucial that refiners keep whatever market share they have."

A round of vicious price-cutting in 1994 was sparked by Ssangyong's effort to secure greater market share regardless of profit. Ssangyong's market share rose slightly at first, but fell back after several months.
